stories.body:
We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise

I n the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world.

In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal.

In 10 days, Donald Trump will enter his own twilight zone. He is almost certain to lose control of the House and it’s not impossible he will face a Democratic Senate too. Any hopes of passing domestic policy – not that he’s bothered with that much during his first two years – will disappear. Instead, he will face a series of investigations that could lead, once again, to impeachment.

On the world stage, however, it will be a different story. And unlike Bush senior, Clinton and Obama, his ambitions won’t be peaceful. The first two years of his second term have been catastrophic; the final two could be even worse.

Once the midterms are over, the US is understood to be planning to restart its unwinnable war with Iran , already carrying out exercises with the Israeli military and withdrawing diplomats from the region. Trump’s sellout of Ukraine is well under way. In the past week he has argued that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”, while his envoy Steve Witkoff met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, praising him in a televised meeting as a “humanitarian…and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.”

On top of a reckless war in the Middle East and appeasement in Europe, the shadow of a new world order is emerging, which Trump will relentlessly pursue in his final years. Putin has proposed a summit between himself, Trump and China’s Xi Jinping , to be held in China next month.

Such an unprecedented meeting, were it to take place, would have potentially devastating consequences for the rest of us. The three leaders have ambitions to transform the way the world is governed, essentially dividing it into spheres of influence. One summit wouldn’t turn an idea into reality, but it would send us down a very dangerous path. In Europe, it would have an impact beyond Ukraine if the US refused to help protect nations threatened by Russia . In east Asia, the withdrawal of the American security blanket would cause enormous problems for Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, as well as Australia.

We’ve talked a lot about the end of the west over the past two years – this feels like a moment when many of those fears will crystalise.

The Trump administration’s ambition to divide the world into spheres and side with dictators over democrats has long been evident. Last year’s National Security Strategy was deeply critical of the US’s traditional allies in Europe and east Asia. But it was what it didn’t say that was most shocking. Both Russia and China avoided direct criticism. In six paragraphs describing the threat to Taiwan, China was not mentioned once. Elsewhere in the document, China was actually praised as “rich and powerful … us[ing] its wealth and power to its considerable advantage.” The section on Russia’s war in Ukraine failed to mention how it started and did not suggest that Putin should be defeated; instead it focused on how the US could help Europe and Russia mend their relationship. The 33-page document discussed the importance of the US controlling the western hemisphere, but made clear that so long as the US still had economic dominance, it cared little whether other parts of the world are protected. “The affairs of other countries,” it stated, “are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests.” For too long, it argued, America’s allies had “suck[ed] us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own”.

For Putin, this is a success almost three decades in the making. He has long viewed American support for democracy in eastern Europe and central Asia as “interference” in Russia’s backyard. Now he has a US president who agrees. Trump has also placed Putin on a far higher pedestal than Russia’s economy and its technological prowess deserves.

Xi, too, has welcomed the US’s rhetorical retreat from east Asia, particularly if it allows China greater maritime control in the East China Sea and South China Sea. World opinion on China has dramatically improved as that of the US has slid. As Chrystia Freeland, a former Canadian foreign minister, put it this week, “there has not been a president who has been more beneficial for China than Donald Trump”.

At stake is not merely territorial control. All three governments see the possibility of increasing economic ties. For the US and China, the bigger issues are future control of economic supply chains and technology platforms, while Russia’s fossil fuel resources are also a factor. All three are key players in the next space race, both in terms of commercial and military control. If these three nations begin to work together, at the expense of Europe and the rest of the world, it will fundamentally change the nature of geopolitics. A decade ago, talk of a multipolar world was based around the idea of the US, China and the European Union as the three most powerful blocs. Somehow, Brussels has been replaced by Moscow.

after newsletter promotion

Until now, the rest of the west has – on the whole – tried to muddle through. Nato still exists on paper, G7 and G20 summits may be chaotic but they still take place. Optimists in the Foreign Office point out that Trump turned up to the UN general assembly and his administration is still deeply involved in the UN’s day to day activities.

Mark Carney spoke of a “rupture” and warned the old post-cold war world was not coming back, but despite warm words from Emmanuel Macron, and renewed discussion about how Europe can protect itself without the US, there is still a sense that everyone is waiting for Trump’s time in office to end. A Great Powers summit makes this harder to ignore.

While US presidents seek foreign policy success in their final months, history suggests they rarely find it. Clinton’s Camp David talks collapsed after Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat were unable to reach an agreement. Bush would argue that his initial intervention in Somalia eased a famine, but it ended in humiliation. A botched raid on a warlord led to the deaths of 18 US soldiers and several hundred Somalis. Obama’s diplomacy in Cuba and Iran succeeded, but were both promptly ripped up by Donald Trump.

Trump will get his photoshoot – and maybe that’s all he wants – but there is no guarantee that this unsavoury troika becomes a permanent geopolitical fixture. Trump’s foreign policy has divided his Maga movement and has shocked traditional conservatives. The Wall Street Journal editorial board described the proposed summit as “arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term”. A President Vance or Rubio might be less willing to throw in their lot with dictators; a President Ossoff or Ocasio-Cortez certainly won’t.

But just because Trump won’t win, doesn’t mean that the US won’t lose. He will be arriving in Shenzhen at the weakest moment in his presidency. An 80-year-old lame duck leader fated to limp towards the finish line unable to pass any legislation and threatened by two chaotic years of investigations into his alleged corruption. Opposite him will be two authoritarian leaders in their early 70s who believe the only thing preventing them from ruling their nations for another two decades is death. Indeed, given their “hot mic” discussions about longevity drugs last year, perhaps they both believe they can rule for even longer.

If it goes ahead, this summit will bring Putin back in from the cold and reiterate Xi’s position as a global leader who cannot be ignored. The image of the three leaders will come to define this era when the rules-based international order was torn apart and a new, uncertain period began to form.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

stories.title: Rocket Report: SpaceX says no thanks to military launches; Spanish rocket nearly ready
stories.summary: "We believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms."

stories.body:
“We believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms.”

Welcome to Edition 9.16 of the Rocket Report! Lots of SpaceX-related news this week including a couple of Thursday shockers. In one story, the company told the US Space Force thanks, but no thanks after being offered three military launch contracts. Then, on the civil space side of things, SpaceX’s Starship may required up to 22 refuelings to support a lunar landing, a NASA safety panel said.

As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

Miura 5 getting closer to launch . PLD Space says its Miura 5 rocket, due to undertake its inaugural launch next year, is nearing final integration, Aviation Week reports . The rocket is one of three Miura 5s the company has already manufactured, with the other two designed to qualify key system elements, CEO Raúl Torres said in an October 19 program update. PLD Space now targets a first flight of the small-lift vehicle before mid-2027.

Fully integrated stage … “Manufacturing these three vehicles has allowed our teams to work continuously across different stages of production and integration, applying the lessons learned from each qualification campaign directly to the launch vehicle,” Torres said. One Miura 5 second stage is now fully integrated to kick off system-level testing under representative operating conditions. The second stage is at PLD’s Teruel test facility for its qualification campaign, including wet dress rehearsal and a static hot-fire test.

Reaction Dynamics seeks to raise $350 million . One of three prominent Canadian launch startups, Reaction Dynamics, said it is seeking to raise $350 million to grow its staff from 68 to more than 350 people, spaceQ reports . The company is developing the small-lift Aurora rocket, which Reaction Dynamics hopes will reach orbit in 2028. Reaction Dynamics also announced plans to build a medium-lift rocket, Borealis, for a debut by 2031.

You’ve got the aurora, and the borealis … With a lift capacity of 6 tons to low-Earth orbit, Borealis would carry a little under half of the advertised payload capacity of Rocket Lab’s Neutron vehicle. “We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,” the company’s founder and chief executive, Bachar Elzein, said. “Aurora is how we get to orbit in 2028. Borealis is how we deliver sovereign access to orbit, at scale, by 2031.” Both of the dates appear to be highly aspirational, but we wish them luck.

Rocket Lab sets next Electron launch date . After 97 launches of Electron, it is not exactly news that Rocket Lab is preparing for its 98th launch of the vehicle. The mission , launching three HAWK satellites for the constellation operator HawkEye 360, is due to launch as early as 07:00 UTC on Friday, October 23.

So why are you writing about it ? … Two reasons. First of all, it’s worth noting that Rocket Lab continues to be only the second company to develop and frequently fly a purely commercial rocket. Secondly, we love the name of the mission, “We’re Not Hawking Around.” Kudos to the Rocket Lab team for keeping launch fun and fresh, even after moving through dozens of launches.

SpaceX says no thanks to Space Force launches . The Space Force recently tried to book rides for three future satellite missions, but SpaceX declined to offer its services, Politico reports . No other rocket companies offered to take them either, the publication reported. A top Space Force official, Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the acting portfolio acquisition executive, acknowledged growing pains for the government and space industry as demand for rockets increases. “Temporarily, there are some things we’ll need to work through, again, as we get new providers flying,” he said. SpaceX has been declining to sign new Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launch contracts for all kinds of customers.

No one else has capacity … The three Space Force missions that didn’t find a ride were listed through the National Security Space Launch initiative. Two of the missions were for the Space Development Agency. The agency is a branch of the Space Force that’s building a network of hundreds of military satellites in low-Earth orbit to provide expanded data services, and missile warning and tracking capabilities. Other potential launch providers, United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin, are both working through setbacks with their launch vehicles. Zarybnisky remained optimistic that Blue Origin and ULA will work through their technical problems and that new competitors will get up and running in time.

Who will win the medium-lift launch race ? It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation. Nearly a decade and a half later, there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine.

Which comes first … In a new article, Ars updates the status of four medium-lift rockets under development in the United States: Stoke Space’s Nova, Relativity Space’s Terran R, Rocket Lab’s Neutron, and the Eclipse vehicle being built by Firefly and Northrop Grumman. The publication also (somewhat hazardously) predicts the order in which the four rockets will make their debut.

Japanese rocket launches historic Phobos mission . Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, Ars reports . The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan.

This has been tried before … The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan’s flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan’s heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. MMX is not the first mission to attempt a sample return from Phobos. Russia’s Phobos-Grunt sample return mission failed soon after launch in 2011, before it could set off for Mars. (submitted by tsunam)

Chinese rocket debris found in Midwest . In September, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest, Ars reports . The rocket’s flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin.

A surprising find … The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before. The incident was largely forgotten until the last few days, when a farmer in rural Minnesota discovered a circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter lay amid the forest of corn stalks.

Arianespace targets Nov. 23 return for Ariane 6 . Arianespace has announced that the next Ariane 6 launch will take place no earlier than November 23, marking the rocket’s return to flight after ground testing reportedly revealed an issue with one of its turbopumps, European Spaceflight reports . The flight will carry 36 Amazon Leo satellites aboard an Ariane 64, the rocket’s four-booster configuration. It will be the fifth Ariane 6 flight of 2026 and the tenth since the rocket’s inaugural flight in July 2024.

Situation is on track … Arianespace’s new announcement follows a report from French newspaper La Tribune, published a day earlier, claiming ArianeGroup had resolved an anomaly affecting a liquid hydrogen turbopump that had disrupted the rocket’s launch schedule. According to the report, the anomaly was first detected during an engine acceptance test shortly before the start of summer. Asked by European Spaceflight to comment on the report, an ArianeGroup spokesperson declined to address it directly and instead pointed to the newly announced launch date. “The next launch has been announced today, so the situation is on track.”

How many Starships will be required for a lunar landing ? On Thursday, the NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel held its quarterly meeting, during which panel member Charlie Precourt (a former NASA astronaut) spoke about risks associated with the Artemis Program and landing humans on the Moon, Ars reports . One of these is the number of refuelings required to support a Starship lunar landing.

Uncertainty remains … “With respect to Artemis IV, however, we’ve got a large number of firsts that reduce the likelihood of mission success,” Precourt said. “We need to keep our eyes on numerous required fuelings for the lander. I think the last estimate is around 22 flights.” In response to this, SpaceX founder Elon Musk replied that NASA’s safety panel estimate was not accurate. “That’s way too high,” Musk said. “Actual number will be more like 6 to 8.”

SpaceX will attempt a rocket and upper stage catch . It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive Starship rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight, Ars reports . SpaceX founder Elon Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures.

Working with the FAA … Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight. One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico. “We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said.

Blue Origin goes bigger on New Glenn . Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its already considerable Florida launch facilities last Friday with the intent of eventually flying more than 100 rockets a year from there, Ars reports . The company said it would add two launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. The company is also investing heavily in a new manufacturing facility that will produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger variant of the New Glenn rocket.

More missions … The company also plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of the New Glenn rocket (it currently has one, named Jacklyn). Finally, Blue Origin said it would add a new customer integration facility, built in conjunction with the US Space Force, that will feature four payload bays to process multiple missions at the same time. “These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,” said Ian Richardson, senior vice president of operations at Blue Origin.

Next three launches

October 23 : Electron | We’re Not Hawking Around | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 07:00 UTC

October 23 : Long March 6A | Unknown payload | Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, China | 10:15 UTC

October 23 : Long March 4B | Unknown payload | Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, China | 19:25 UTC

stories.title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
stories.summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Canada and the US are currently locked in a tit-for-tat trade war

Published 23 October 2026

The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.

From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.

Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.

The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".

Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.

The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".

It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".

Maine Senator Susan Collins is seeking to keep her seat in November's midterm elections

Trump "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce", White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said.

Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."

The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term.

Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner".

The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts Published 31 August

She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".

Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."

Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.

Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.

Also on Friday, Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US.

Carney, who has sought closer ties with Europe since the tariff war erupted, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but was willing to wait it out.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that."

LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.

Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).

The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.

Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .

Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.

Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.

Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.

Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

stories.title: 'My daughter's bed was propped up on books,' says mum amid child poverty fears
stories.summary: Sarah Ruscoe, a single mum out of work due to health issues, worried her daughter’s bed would collapse at night.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sarah Ruscoe's daughter Sabrina is among Wales' one-third of children living in relative poverty

Published 24 October 2026, 14:39 BST

"I was sleeping on the sofa, she had a bed that was propped up on books. One of the legs had fallen off completely."

Sarah Ruscoe, a single mum out of work because of a health condition, said she had worried her daughter's bed would collapse in the night after finding herself in a "dire" financial situation.

A food bank user, Ruscoe said "every year seems to be getting worse" as she struggled to make her benefits cover essentials.

A charity eventually paid for a new bed for daughter Sabrina, 11.

But MPs heard this week that the general picture of one in three children living in relative poverty in Wales had not changed in 20 years, with a think tank saying the problem was becoming entrenched.

'There's so much I want to give my daughter - poverty means I can't' Published 27 April

£10-a-week child poverty payment plans faces obstacles, says expert Published 9 July

On Wednesday MPs at the UK Parliament's Welsh Affairs Committee opened an inquiry on ending child poverty in Wales.

The country has the highest child poverty rate of any UK nation, with 32% of children living in relative poverty after housing costs, according to the latest official statistics.

A child is considered to be in relative poverty if the income of the household they live in is below 60% of the UK median.

Evidence was given by charities including Action for Children, who paid for Sabrina's new bed and provides financial support to thousands of low income families in Wales each year.

Ruscoe, from Barry, told BBC Wales that three years ago she struggled to afford to replace her daughter's "ropey" bed which had been "second or third hand".

"It was getting a bit distressing," she said, and both mother and daughter had worried it might collapse in the night when Sabrina moved.

"I was having difficulty finding somewhere where I could afford one, and also not having the greatest credit rating in the world meant that you had to pay like two or three times what you would have done if you'd just gone into a shop and bought it outright."

The new bed meant Sabrina had "somewhere safe" to sleep, her mother says

The cabin bunk and a mattress purchased by Action for Children made a "massive difference", she said.

"It meant she had somewhere safe. It's a little nest now. We decorated it," Ruscoe said.

"Nobody else has slept in it. It's something that's new for her.

"Up until that point it was worry and trying to work out, maybe if I didn't pay this bill maybe I could save some money here, what could I go without, trying to work out which company had the smallest APR on an item that I could afford.

"There's not that much out there, especially when they hear you're on benefits."

One year the charity also helped the family with a gift card for local supermarkets before Christmas.

Ruscoe, who used to work in a job centre, said her chronic pain condition fibromyalgia had left her feeling fatigued and in pain and, when it had flared up, unable to move.

"I don't work due to my disabilities so it's a case of benefits, and that's how we survive, and this year seems to be worse than last year. Every year seems to be getting worse.

"Last year I managed to put money away over the course of the year for Christmas and this year I haven't been able to at all. Everything has gone up.

"There's only so much penny pinching you can do on everything and then realise that every penny you've pinched is still not covering all your bills and your outgoings."

The mother and daughter are just one of hundreds of families who have received financial help from Action for Children

Ruscoe warned that anyone could find themselves in a crisis situation because of ill-health or an unexpected life event.

Laurie Ryall, Wales director at Action for Children, gave evidence to MPs on the first day of their inquiry in Westminster, and said the absence of a single point of access for support had often left families experiencing child poverty feeling overwhelmed.

"They don't always know what they're entitled to or where to go, it's confusing, it's a minefield," Ryall said.

Mabli Jones from the Bevan Foundation think tank told MPs that although child poverty had remained at the same level for two decades "what's been happening under the surface is that poverty has got deeper".

"Almost half - 47% - of people in Wales who live in poverty live in what's classed as very deep poverty - that's an income that is at or below 40% of the median," she said.

"Families who are experiencing that kind of poverty are likely to be going without many of the basics."

A UK government spokesperson said: "We're determined to turn the tide on poverty, and our landmark child poverty strategy will lift 550,000 children out of poverty in the final year of this parliament - the largest reduction in child poverty since records began."

They said abolishing the two-child limit would benefit an estimated 69,000 children in Wales, and a temporary cut to electricity bills and raising the National Living Wage had contributed to a fall in food bank usage.

A Welsh government spokesperson said it had "inherited a damning legacy of stubbornly high levels of child poverty".

It said it was helping families through the first phase of its offer of 12.5 hours of free childcare to all two-year-olds and extending free school meals.

They also said the government was seeking assurance from the UK government that a proposed pilot scheme for £10 a week to each child to support low-income families would not affect families' benefit payments.

"We continue to call on the UK government to use all the levers at its disposal, including those on welfare, to make a lasting difference to families in Wales," they said.

stories.body:
If you use the internet at all, you may have noticed that a large percentage of sites suddenly went down earlier this week — and all your nerdiest friends were talking about "The Vulnerability Apocalypse” and this thing called PHP that powers nearly 70% of the websites on the internet . You may find yourself wondering: what is PHP, what just happened, what is the vulnerability apocalypse, and what do I need to do?

To find out what you can personally do read the first blog post in this series!

What Is PHP?

PHP is a programming language used mainly to create interactive websites. Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. But because it is open-source, maintenance of these critical systems depends on a small number of volunteers working on this in their free time. The disaster scenario that happened this past week is the perfect example of why we need more money and people supporting open-source projects. Corporations should be contributing both.

What Is the Vulnerability Apocalypse?

Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) are the way that security professionals file reports about vulnerabilities in software. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD), run by NIST, is the official national database of CVEs. In other words, CVE reports managed by NIST are the closest thing we have to a canonical database of security vulnerabilities in software. The NVD currently has around 400,000 CVEs that have been filed and accepted since 1988. In just the month of October, 13,000 new CVEs have been submitted. This means that 3% of critical software security bugs that have ever been officially logged were found in the last month alone. And it's likely that by the end of the year over a quarter of the software vulnerabilities that have ever been found will be from 2026.

Computer vulnerabilities reported are rising exponentially. Source: CVE Tracker

This research is being driven almost entirely by the cybersecurity capabilities of major AI models from companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Historically it has been popularly assumed by cybersecurity experts that finding unknown (zero-day) exploits in any specific project and turning them into exploits was expensive. The knowledge to discover them was not widespread, and it was a hard task even for those initiated into the arcane ways of vulnerability hunting. Google even dedicated an entire team to it .

But now thanks to major AI models, vulnerabilities are cheap, and anyone of moderate technical skill with a few dollars and access to a frontier AI model can find vulnerabilities in a few minutes. For example, recent vulnerabilities in PHP were found with a prompt to an AI model that literally said " find bad vulnerabilities in PHP ."

What Happened This Week?

In 2024, a potentially severe vulnerability in PHP was discovered during an external security audit . PHP’s maintainers couldn’t agree on a solution, but more importantly, they couldn’t find a way to exploit the vulnerability. Because it didn’t seem like an active threat, they ended up deprioritizing a fix in favor of working on more urgent security issues. Then, in August 2026, security researchers working with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic independently discovered the vulnerability again, and another one — and now, with a way to exploit them.

We now know that the vulnerabilities were so severe that they would have allowed even moderately inventive hackers to take over any website that uses PHP and then steal customer data, launch further malware attacks, spy on users, take websites offline, or launch a massive denial of service attack. [ 1 ]

Because of the severity of these vulnerabilities, several of the involved researchers got together with the makers of PHP to patch the vulnerabilities and disclose them in a coordinated manner. The idea was that hopefully everyone would get a chance to quietly release and then apply fixes for the vulnerabilities before the whole world found out about it.

But news already started to leak on October 20th. There was a post on a widely read forum “Hacker News” and other posts elsewhere. One of the researchers accidentally published a video early. Companies reported seeing active exploitation of the vulnerabilities going back as far as October 17th. On October 21st, six hours before the planned press embargo, one company, Chainguard, jumped the gun and released a patch early, essentially giving anyone instructions about exactly where to find the vulnerabilities and how to weaponize them. This sent system administrators everywhere scrambling to patch their systems before they were taken over by hackers. And it’s going to take a long time to patch all these systems. At the time of this writing over 33 million websites are still running on vulnerable versions of PHP .

The internet is run largely on open-source software, mostly maintained by a small handful of skilled volunteers occasionally getting a small stipend, not by major corporations and highly paid engineers. These are projects you have perhaps never heard of, like PHP, OpenSSL, and SQLite, but these programs run on nearly every computer in the world and are maintained by teams as small as one person. When a vulnerability is found in these projects, it can be devastating.

PHP isn’t the only critical open-source software with a high severity vulnerability this week either. Other widespread open-source projects like Node.js and GitLab also had severe security bugs reported.

The small number of already overworked open-source maintainers are now facing a deluge of vulnerability reports, some of which are false, but many of which are very real. Burnout in open source has never been higher .

We Need Stronger Support for Open Source Projects

Much of the foundation for the modern multibillion-dollar internet industry is built on open-source products that were created and still maintained — for free — by dedicated volunteers in their spare time. It’s an imperfect system, and it can lead to errors.

One of those critical, under resourced open-source products is PHP. And while vulnerabilities in PHP were privately found years ago, they were left unfixed because they didn’t seem as impactful as other bugs at the time. These same vulnerabilities were recently rediscovered and proved to be trivially exploitable by security researchers using advanced AI models. While in the middle of the widespread, global effort to correct this mistake and deploy fixes, the problem was leaked by some of the security researchers who had gotten early access to the fixes. Unfortunately, this left millions of websites, ranging from personal blogs to government sites, vulnerable to hacking that could result in data theft, malware distribution, and worse.

Open-source projects like PHP and others are the backbone of the entire internet. If they don’t get the resources they need, they and the internet they power, are at risk of falling apart. Corporations (whose products would not exist without these products) should be actively contributing to their maintenance.

It is a commonly held truth among computer geeks that there is no such thing as bug free software, or a secure computer. Any piece of software that anyone actually uses will have a security vulnerability somewhere in the code . The more complex that software is, the more likely there will be a vulnerability. Fortunately for everyone, finding severe vulnerabilities was generally considered an expensive and difficult task requiring years of training and deep knowledge of how computers and software worked. Until recently there was a steady background hum of vulnerabilities being found and patched, with major vulnerabilities that could cripple the entire internet only happening every few years. Now that is no longer the case.

You may have noticed your nerdiest friends freaking out about the “Vulnerability Apocalypse” this week and waving their arms in panic about something called PHP. You may have also noticed that some of your favorite websites were down for a bit. In the last two weeks of October alone, there have been multiple, potentially internet-breaking vulnerabilities reported and patched. Many of those vulnerabilities were in the open-source software that is the foundation of the vast majority of the internet.

For more detailed information on what happened, and why supporting open-source projects matters, check out our other blog .

This is all because frontier AI models, such as those created by OpenAI, Anthropic, and others, have made it incredibly cheap and easy to find previously unknown vulnerabilities (zero-days) in open- and closed-source code. Three percent of all software vulnerabilities ever found in history were found just in the month of October. This year alone researchers have found nearly a quarter of all software security issues which have ever been discovered.

If exploiting critical software is now cheaper and easier than ever, what does that mean for us as individuals and what does that mean for society as a whole? TL; DR : It’s going to get worse before it gets better. But you can protect yourself with basic digital security hygiene that is now more important than ever.

What Do I Need to Do?

There absolutely needs to be a bigger conversation about how we got here and how to fix the systemic issues involved, including how corporations that depend on open-source code should contribute to their upkeep, and how big tech should be regulated.

But for now, this news is a compelling reason to tighten up your digital hygiene. A lot of computers are going to get hacked a lot more often, and unfortunately, it isn’t going to get better any time soon. Thankfully, EFF has compiled a comprehensive set of security advice in our Surveillance Self-Defense guides . To start , we recommend making sure your browser and all applications are always up to date with the latest patches.

You should also consider installing a tracker blocking tool, like EFF’s Privacy Badger ( now on Safari ), and remain vigilant for phishing attempts . Additionally, install a password manager and use unique passwords for each website, so that if one site is compromised, the rest of your passwords are safe. You should also be aware that data breaches may now be more likely, and the websites you visit may experience more attacks than usual, which means that some services may be disrupted.

If you host a blog or other website, make sure that either you or your hosting provider has patched this particular issue.

For additional tips on protecting yourself and others, head over to our Surveillance Self-Defense site . Additionally, if you’d like to support any of EFF’s open-source projects like Privacy Badger , Rayhunter , and Certbot , visit our donate page .

stories.title: Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test
stories.summary: The prime minister might be dreaming of gold medals in 2040, but he must first navigate the difficult years in between, writes Laura Kuenssberg.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test

Published 7 hours ago

Giving the north of England a crack at hosting the globe's biggest sports event might seem about as Brand Burnham as it gets.

Seven million pounds of taxpayers' cash is a teeny drop in the context of the overall Budget, to pay for the government to take a closer look at possible plans. But the idea is sure to get tongues wagging - and headline writers scribbling.

A "Northern Games" in 2040 or beyond just might create a massive sense of national feel-good, jobs and development, as the Olympics in east London did more than a decade ago.

But it's a promise of a possibility at least a decade away. And what could be more in tune with the Manchester-loving prime minister and his proud Yorkshireman chancellor than a sporting plan fixed firmly on the top geographical chunk of the country?

Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget Published 3 hours ago

It's Brand Burnham alright, popular with most of the Labour backbenches, just add the Twiglets and the pint in the stands.

The prime minister and his team are proud of a distinct feature of their government so far, focusing on small things that might make a big difference: fines for blaring out music on your phone on the bus, cracking down on "rip-off" parking charges, investing a small amount of cash in a big ambition for a sporting event in future.

It's what some ministers call "the politics of trying" – putting time and effort into ideas that you don't pretend are revolutionary, but give direction, and a sense of sympathy to the public.

It's an echo, deliberate or not, of another Labour Prime Minister, Harold Wilson, who sent memos to his cabinet in 1974 demanding "little things that mean a lot".

He ended up with a list of plans including nationalising small breweries to stop them being gulped up by big firms (paging Andy Burnham), freezing phone installation charges for pensioners, and plans for empty office blocks.

But the next few days could bring an end to that "politics of trying" phase, with one senior official describing the coming Budget as "the first proper moment for the government, which will then be in the pipeline for the 10-year plan, then a very difficult spending review".

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

An influential Labour MP told me: "The Budget has to be the beginning of the future story."

A fancy way of saying, beyond the short-term announcements and clear long-term aspirations, what is this government actually going to do?

"Steady as she goes," is what one well-connected senior MP predicts, and how expectations of the Budget are being managed across Westminster. They tell me: "Not doing a lot might be more reassuring to people than promising the earth with whose money?"

The boss of one well-known high street business told me they are even hoping there won't be any big bazookas. "Just do no harm," they implored the Chancellor John Healey.

"The hole is too big that they are trying to fill, so my view is don't try and do anything big to help because you don't have the money, but don't do anything to harm us either."

After all, the chancellor is bound by Labour's manifesto promises not to fiddle with the main taxes – income tax, VAT, National Insurance for workers. And you don't need me to remind you that public spending, borrowing and tax are all at historic highs.

Chuck in prices jacking up again because of war in the Middle East and there isn't much money to spray around. In fact, some big cuts to public spending are already pencilled in for the later years of this parliament.

The chancellor and prime minister face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending

But the widespread suggestion that you'll be able to blink and miss the Budget has got some hackles up in the Treasury. A budget, by its very nature, can never be a small event - it sets billions upon billions of taxes and spending decisions.

And there are likely to be extra taxes on banks, vows to sweep away some business regulation, particularly for small business, more powers passing to local leaders under the guise of devolution and more action on energy bills which are heading back up again.

John Healey has made it clear publicly and to staff, that he wants to encourage people with the guts and drive to start a business. One source said: "If you are taking on John's mantra about talking up Britain then you can't say, 'Nothing to see here'."

Whatever else the chancellor brings to Parliament in his red box, do not expect him to arrive with all the solutions to the country's very well-documented problems, whether that's getting the economy growing more convincingly, sorting out gaps in defence cash, welfare, social care, or new ways to pay off the country's groaning debts more quickly.

One former minister suggests even if Healey and Burnham had stumbled upon all the answers in a few months, it's just not possible to fix everything at the same time because of the constraints on the economy.

They wondered: "Is he going to invest in growth? Is he going to put everything he has into the challenges people will face this winter? Is he going to throw it at defence? There is just not enough to tackle all these problems simultaneously - ministers are going to be exposed to the cold light of day."

Burnham and Healey have to find a way of maintaining the balance in an unusually happy Labour Party.

MPs talk of ministers and Burnham himself being more visible and approachable in Parliament, knocking around with colleagues in the evening, fewer "golden slips" doled out when ministers were excused from voting alongside colleagues so they could get on with their important jobs.

One minister told me they'd had to tell their private office not to arrange for them to be "slipped" , from going to the Commons in the evening to see backbenchers.

It's paying off in the mood among MPs. One told me: "You're not feeling like the only way you can ever have a chat with a minister is by arranging an appointment for three months down the line – the soft touches really matter."

Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October

A party that feels the boss has their back is more likely to be receptive to hard decisions, that's simple psychology, and guess what? Politicians are humans too.

But the equilibrium is fragile. One source involved in the Budget prep told me the government "is like a seesaw".

"It's John and James on the right (Healey and Purnell, Burnham's chief of staff), Lou (Haigh) on the left, and Andy balancing it in the middle," adding that "Andy is not as on the left as many of his supporters want to believe".

That balance could be more strained in the coming weeks as choices over immigration and welfare reform loom after the Budget. And how the numbers stack up on Wednesday matters intensely too.

The Labour left will be looking keenly to see if people who are really struggling financially receive meaningful support.

Those on the right will be scouring the statement for measures that display a tight control on spending and help businesses grow. Even small moves could upset the seesaw.

One former minister doubts there will be anything major enough to upset the delicate balance, not because of an abundance of caution but they suggest, "John has been struggling a bit - he hasn't gone into this with a philosophical direction".

There is also a risk that by deferring big decisions until the Spending Review next year - which sets out longer-term spending than an annual budget - it looks like the government is just putting off the hard stuff.

Another acknowledges the danger of looking like it's a budget on the never-never, delaying decisions on "welfare, defence and social care – Andy goes in with political stock quite high – he needs to spend it on difficult stuff and there isn't much sign of it yet".

In an interview with The Times, Andy Haldane, a former chief economist at the Bank of England and an ally of Burnham, said he feared the government would deliver a "mañana budget" that deferred difficult decisions on public spending and "doesn't speak to the urgency of now".

With friends like these…

The former mayor of Greater Manchester became the UK's fourth prime minister in five years and the seventh since 2016

It's a good bet that the opposition parties will pile in on this angle, accusing Healey and Burnham of ignoring the long-term pressures next week. One prominent opposition politician said: "This Budget can only be postponing, you have to assume that's cynical because you are going to have an early election, or you are storing up a car crash for next year (the Spending Review)."

Downing Street sources counter that argument with Burnham's decision to unpick the expensive triple lock to pay, at least in part, for future social care. Or his bolder approach to potentially ask to re-enter the EU, or certainly pursue much closer ties.

And remember that list of small things that could make a big difference? They have made political decisions that the polls suggest voters have noticed.

Even some of Burnham's backers admit quietly that he is aware his first job in office was clear: to show action, to cheer up his party, and that seems to have had a positive effect in the polls.

His long-term view of the UK he wants is well known – with devolution, a national care service, and greater public involvement in the economy.

But the middle bit?

One official says: "Unless the prime minister has said something quite specific about something everyone is scrambling around trying to work out what he wants to do."

Another well-connected source says: "The challenge has always been with this project, how do people feel in the medium term – it's huge."

​​Burnham and his chancellor's start in office has been broadly successful if you look at the polling, or read the mood inside the Labour party.

Their dreams of future glories, long-term plans and policies, and gold medals on UK soil could point ahead to many years time.

But neither deal with the issues that need to be confronted in the middle.

The chancellor was working late in his Downing Street flat last night, finishing off his plans after having fish pie for tea, conscious his first Budget starts the between times - and they're almost here.

An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude

In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.

“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.

A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.

Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.

In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare.

The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France , India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee.

Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern , with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.”

Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.”

Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied : “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?”

Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways.

“The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said.

Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits . While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College.

“Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.”

In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.

Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products.

If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement.

In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE.

Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise.

The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods.

Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

stories.body:
Economic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budget

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

The latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “ Burnham bounce ”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey.

Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: “Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”

It comes as consumers face a fresh squeeze on living standards triggered by the unfolding war in the Middle East. Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills have increased in advance of a difficult winter for households already feeling the pinch from years of price increases.

Over the past five years analysis by the Trades Union Congress shows that UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.

With less than a week before his tax and spending speech to the Commons, the chancellor is under pressure to take action to support households amid warnings that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household.

Healey has pledged to use his statement to announce “breathing space” measures to ease the pressure. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the Middle East conflict pushes the UK’s borrowing costs to the highest level in decades.

Official figures released on Wednesday show headline inflation rose by more than expected to 3.5% last month , while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn.

In a double blow for the chancellor, the twin pieces of bad news underscore the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.

According to the latest figures from GfK, consumers became less confident about the strength of their own personal finances, as well as the general outlook for the British economy at large.

The major purchase index fell by 14 points to -22 in October, suggesting that consumers could be bracing to cut back on spending over the winter months to make room in their finances for higher energy bills.

Separate figures from the CBI show investment intentions among manufacturing businesses were subdued as cost pressures remained high in the three months to October.

Manufacturing output is expected to stabilise in the next three months, according to the lobby group’s latest Industrial Trends Survey. However, cost pressures for businesses remained elevated.

Cameron Martin, senior economist at the CBI, said: “If the government wants to meaningfully tackle the cost of living, it must give manufacturers the breathing space to invest and drive the productivity growth needed to sustain rising real wages.

“Next week’s budget must deliver this by cutting business electricity costs, reducing labour costs and reforming business rates to support rather than hinder investment and growth.”

The Treasury has been approached for comment.

stories.body:
The NHS has a substantial carbon footprint . Yet one part of its environmental impact receives relatively little attention: maternity care.

The health service is responsible for an estimated 4% to 5% of England’s greenhouse gas emissions . A 2025 report from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists estimated that selected maternity care activities in England generated about 205,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in 2022–23.

CO₂e expresses the warming effect of different greenhouse gases, such as methane, as an equivalent amount of carbon dioxide. The analysis excluded some maternity services, so the total footprint is likely to be higher.

Nearly 29% of the emissions across the activities studied came from Entonox, commonly known as gas and air. It contains nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas. Using it during regular contractions over four hours has an estimated warming effect of 237kg CO₂e .

Travel to appointments also contributes to emissions. An analysis at the Whittington , a hospital in north London, estimated that a patient’s return journey to an antenatal appointment generated an average of 1.23kg CO₂e.

Hospitals also use large quantities of disposable equipment . Ready-to-use formula bottles and teats, single-use cups and clinical waste containers are routinely used once and discarded.

Pregnancy is sometimes described as a “teachable moment” , when people may be particularly receptive to health information. Environmental advice could become part of those conversations, including discussions about feeding a baby or choosing pain relief.

Responsibility for reducing emissions

But placing responsibility on parents creates ethical problems. Maternity care in the UK is already under intense pressure. The 2022 Ockenden review documented serious failures in maternity safety, while the 2024 birth trauma inquiry highlighted how women’s concerns were dismissed or ignored.

Read more: Maternity care needs more than answers: it needs change

Against that background, asking someone in labour to weigh the climate effects of pain relief alongside their comfort and safety could create another burden at an already demanding time.

Measuring emissions can help hospitals improve how services are designed. But carbon targets should not be used to restrict access to caesarean birth or pain relief. Decisions about care should respect each person’s needs and informed choices.

In a small interview study involving 12 people who had used nitrous oxide during labour, most wanted environmental information to be available during pregnancy. However, they were unsure whether knowing its impact would change their choice of pain relief. Participants also considered reducing emissions to be primarily the responsibility of healthcare organisations.

A more useful approach is to change how maternity services are delivered while protecting patient choice.

Some NHS maternity services are already doing this. At Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals, a project introduced virtual ward support and care at home for patients with severe pregnancy sickness. By reducing hospital stays, it cut emissions by an estimated 538kg CO₂e over one month. The team projected an annual saving of around 6,462kg if those reductions continued.

Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust has introduced technology that captures exhaled gas and air and breaks down the nitrous oxide into nitrogen and oxygen, allowing women to continue using gas and air during labour while reducing its environmental impact.

Other changes involve purchasing and waste. Thousands of ready-to-use plastic formula bottles and teats are used in maternity care. A 2019 letter from Irish researchers published in the British Medical Journal highlighted waste from unconsumed formula and discarded packaging. Reducing this could lower emissions without restricting access to formula for those who need or choose it.

Similar questions apply to disposable products throughout maternity wards. Clinicians work in systems designed around single-use equipment and established waste procedures. Changing those systems is likely to be more effective than expecting individual clinicians to improvise greener alternatives.

At the midwife-led White Horse birth centre in Swindon, staff have replaced plastic containers used to dispose of placentas with alternatives made from 96% paper , reducing plastic use and costs.

Breastfeeding illustrates how complicated individual responsibility can become. Compared with exclusive formula feeding, exclusive breastfeeding for six months has been estimated to have a carbon footprint 95kg to 153kg CO₂e lower per baby.

But feeding decisions depend on health and personal circumstances, including the support available to parents. A more useful approach would be to provide effective support for anyone who wants to breastfeed, while reducing unnecessary waste and emissions from the way formula is purchased, prepared and supplied by maternity services.

Better care, lower emissions

The Green Maternity Challenge , part of a programme led by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, brought together nine NHS teams to test ways of reducing emissions while improving maternity care. Several projects involved redesigning services to make treatment easier to access or reduce unnecessary hospital stays.

Better care and lower emissions can go together. But treating sustainability only as a fortunate side effect risks overlooking opportunities to design maternity services deliberately around lower-carbon care.

Hospitals should examine where their emissions come from and give staff the knowledge and resources to reduce them. Changes to purchasing and waste systems, alongside suitable lower-emission technologies, can help services become greener while protecting safe care and informed choice.

Childbirth will always carry an environmental footprint. Health services have the responsibility and practical means to reduce the impact through changes to how care is organised and delivered. Those changes should protect choices without placing additional burdens on the person giving birth.

stories.body:
Several characters have worn the mantle of the villain Clayface in DC comics across eight decades – but the two most prominent must surely be Basil Karlo and Matt Hagen.

Karlo, the first Clayface, who debuted in June 1940, was a B-movie actor who had no superpowers but did have a thirst for blood and a penchant for crime. In the 1950s Batman adventures, Clayface reappeared in the shape of Matt Hagen, a treasure hunter whose accidental encounter with radioactive material gave him the power to transform into a lumbering mass of muddy goo with superhuman strength and the ability to shapeshift into any likeness.

Other comic book versions of Clayface have come and gone over the decades, but for his big screen debut DC has opted to bring back Matt Hagen once again. This time Clayface is centre stage in a supervillain origin story, with a generous helping of body horror – a sub genre that has enjoyed renewed popularity in recent years.

In the film’s contemporary reimagining, Hagen is a Hollywood actor whose career high is ended when his face is brutally disfigured by mobsters in revenge for sleeping with their gang boss’s girlfriend. A desperate Hagen decides to put himself forward as a human guinea pig for the testing of an experimental formula containing microscopic AI.

This treatment promises to regrow damaged cells and repair the body to its original form. At first the results are promising, but then, in response to emotional excitement – especially anger – his flesh begins to warp and take on an unpredictable life of its own.

Following the comics, Hagen learns to shift his malleable face to mimic others. He uses these new abilities in a gory revenge rampage on the gangsters that assaulted him and wrecked his career.

While Clayface doesn’t live up to its genre-bending promise of a comic book body horror, it’s not an unmitigated disaster. The film is entertaining and features enough imaginative sequences to forgive some of its more prosaic and one-dimensional aspects.

I was excited at the prospect of a supervillain story from writer and director Mike Flanagan. The horror impresario is responsible for some brilliant recent adaptations, including the peerless Haunting of Hill House for Netflix. I was also hugely impressed with his risk-taking, imaginative update of Stephen King’s debut novel Carrie. However, Flanagan stepped back from the lead writing role – likely because of scheduling conflicts with Carrie.

He retains a co-writing credit. But there’s little in this film that recalls Flanagan’s sensitivity for character and the nuanced dialogue of his best work. A full rewrite by British-Iranian screenwriter Hossein Amini (the excellent Drive, the not-so-excellent The Snowman) may be partly responsible for the film’s tonal uncertainty and an oddly noncommittal feel to much of the action.

The finished product seems to be grappling with the daring originality of its premise and the need for mainstream appeal.

A strong lead for thin material

That said, Clayface’s lead, Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, carries the weaker aspects of the script extremely well with an admirable commitment to his character’s horrific transformations. The film’s best scenes show Hagen confronting what could either be seen as an exciting new body with superhuman abilities or a terrifying total degeneration.

Harries’ energetic performance produces some memorable sequences where Hagen wrestles with his unruly body, the best of which features a battle to keep his dysfunctional, goopy eyelids from sealing shut. Prosthetic effects are blended effectively with CGI – and horror fans should enjoy the effort and commitment from both the actor and the effects crew.

There are distinct shades of Coralie Fargeat’s outrageous and brilliant mainstream body horror breakthrough The Substance (2024). Clayface shares that relentlessly gory film’s interest in the shallow vanity of celebrity and the lengths the protagonist goes to in order to preserve youth and beauty in a skin-deep world.

Also, the connection between Hagen’s emotional state and his progressively warping flesh results in an interesting exploration of male mental health and its impact on the physical body. That a supervillain origin story tackles these kinds of themes is in itself quite admirable.

Clayface also has strong echoes of David Cronenberg’s masterful and influential piece of body horror The Fly (1986). In this classic, Jeff Goldblum’s scientist accidentally splices his DNA with that of a housefly. His transformation begins as a thrilling set of new abilities before becoming a full bodily breakdown into a grotesque creature.

Clayface aims to tread similar terrain, but simply can’t replicate Cronenberg’s ability to walk the line between terror and wonder at the body’s strange transformations.

The main obstacle to Clayface’s success, however, is the surface-level characterisation and very basic sketching of the supporting ensemble of cliched and cartoonish mobster types. This is most glaring in the eye-rolling love story thrown in to encourage emotional connection with the central characters.

This is something The Fly managed to pull off around the horror as scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) and science journalist Veronica “Ronnie” Quaife (Geena Davis) fall in love and try to defy the odds stacked against them. Theirs is an incredibly convincing performance of chemistry, which was certainly helped by the fact the two actors were dating. Sadly, Clayface just can’t replicate it.

While Clayface’s goriest sequences are full of the imaginative horror that only an enthusiast of the genre could conceive, its dialogue and character remains thin. The movie offers neither the emotional nuance typical of Flanagan at his best nor leans knowingly into the over-the-top tropes of gangsters or the mythology of the comics.

Instead, Clayface falls in a passable middle ground that may be overly tame for horror fans accustomed to the wild spectacles of Fargeat and Cronenberg’s work while also being overly icky and violent for comic book film fans.
