stories.body:
What comes after the dissolution of the liberal world order.

Alden Young is an associate professor of history and global affairs at Yale University. He was a 2021-22 Berggruen Institute Fellow.

Muez Ali is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University in Qatar and honorary research fellow at University College London.

This work is supported by the Cross-Border Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT) research program, funded by UK International Development. The views and opinions expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the UK government.

Sudan has often served as a mirror for judging the health of the liberal world order because it has repeatedly been a laboratory for multilateral interventions to prevent atrocities and stabilize the humanitarian situation.

During the second Sudanese civil war, which stretched from 1983 to 2005, an estimated more than two million people died. In Darfur during the first decade of the 2000s, international observers estimated that 300,000 people died and another 2-3 million people were displaced.

At the time, finding a solution to Sudan’s conflicts was a priority for the United States and the coalitions it galvanized. For instance, Sudan’s second civil war came to an end only after intense mediation by the troika of the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway, as well as Sudan’s African neighbors, in 2005. The level of Western concern and diplomatic resources mobilized to intervene in Sudan’s conflicts in the early 2000s feels almost unimaginable today.

In the 2000s, Sudan hosted two massive UN peacekeeping missions : the more than 13-year-long African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, which ended in 2020 and the more than six-year-long United Nations Mission in the Sudan, which ended in 2011. The goals of these missions were to prevent genocide in Darfur and to guarantee the implementation of the peace agreement ending the civil war between the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement/Army and the government in Khartoum. This mission, which included approximately 10,000 soldiers and numerous civilian authorities, ended with a referendum on the independence of South Sudan in 2011. A few months later South Sudan was welcomed by the international community as the newest country in the world.

It was in this context — of the international efforts to end Sudan’s civil wars and the resulting mass displacements — that South Sudanese diplomat Francis Mading Deng developed the idea of “ sovereignty as responsibility .” Deng served as the Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General on internally displaced persons from 1992 to 2004, and many experts credit Deng’s idea of sovereignty as responsibility as the intellectual genesis of the international principle of the Responsibility to Protect . The UN General Assembly’s adoption of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principles in 2005 marked a high-water point for the legitimacy of the liberal world order. R2P, as formulated by Deng and others, tried to balance sovereignty as a state’s right to non-interference with the international community’s duty to ensure that a state protects the welfare of its own citizens.

Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm. The numbers are massive and stark, making it hard to comprehend the magnitude of the tragedy unfolding there. At least 14 million people have been internally displaced since the latest round of fighting in April 2023, according to the United Nations Refugee Agency. Meanwhile, there are at least 4.4 million Sudanese refugees who have fled the country, many to neighboring countries like Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, which can ill-afford to support this influx. Three years on, intense fighting persists in Sudan’s central region of Kordofan, in Darfur and in its southeastern Blue Nile state.

In one of the most widely discussed recent commentaries on the crisis in Sudan — a conflict often overshadowed despite its horrific violence by other wars — the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum wrote that “no statistics can express the sense of pointlessness, of meaninglessness, that the war has left behind” after she reported from behind the lines of both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and their opponents, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In the face of the physical destruction of cities like Khartoum, Applebaum declared the conflict the most nihilistic on Earth, writing with a tinge of hopelessness that “the liberal world order has already ended in Sudan, and there isn’t anything to replace it.”

In many ways, what is happening in Sudan represents the international community’s abandonment of the longstanding principles of the liberal world order, particularly by the West. Instead, Sudan has become the plaything for a wide array of actors stretching across the Middle East and Africa, to Russia and Ukraine, and as far afield as Colombia. After the Trump administration’s cuts to organizations like the U.S. Agency for International Development, even the commitment to prevent the spread of famine has declined. Applebaum ended her piece by lamenting that Sudan is now a victim of an anarchic, post-American world. A world that has yet to fully take shape in which “colonialism is long past, the Cold War has ended,” and the international order has irreparably broken down.

“Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm.”

But what is taking place in Sudan and elsewhere is not the emergence of anarchy; it is a return to precolonial patterns. Many observers have mistakenly assumed the former because of what the historian Richard Reid calls the “ foreshortening of African history ,” by which he means “the detachment of Africa’s turbulent present — and its recent past — from deeper patterns of both change and continuity.” Perhaps no country has suffered more from the reification of the colonial past by social scientists and modernizing elites alike than the Congo, once known as Zaire.

At the end of the 19th century, Henry Morten Stanley earned the name Bula Matari or the breaker of rocks, for “his feat of driving a caravan of porters bearing dismantled steamers over the torturous terrain between the Zaire River estuary and the vast navigable watercourses extending inward from Kinshasa.” As Zala Lusibu N’Kanza, the first woman to hold the position of minister in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, notes, “for all Bakongo the name of Bula Matari signified terror.” The precolonial was smashed in the wake of an ascendant and modernizing colonial and post-colonial state. For the founding generation of American political scientists like the late Crawford Young, the political, economic and social institutions of the precolonial period were left in ruins because they lacked the resilience to create an alternative to the modernizing state.

A Return To The Pre-Colonial Era

Despite the depths of the human tragedy playing out across northeast Africa — engulfing not only Sudan but South Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia and Somaliland — Applebaum’s post-American world is not just chaos. Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era. The long dominance of the colonial state was not the result of smashing African societies, as American political scientists long suspected. Just as the chaos marring the post-colonial period is not a result of ethnic rivalries. Rather, the endurance of colonialism in countries like Sudan is a product of the legacies of its infrastructure.

The peculiar durability of the infrastructure built during European control of the Nile basin resulted from a set of historical conjunctures. In his new book, “The Alibi of Capital: How We Broke the Earth to Steal the Future on the Promise of a Better Tomorrow,” the political theorist Timothy Mitchell argues that around the turn of the 20th century a new ability to discount the future was invented. Mitchell considers this ability a political technology “derived from the fact that time can be controlled — by the construction of a political apparatus that will reliably capture and colonize the future.” While this sounds incredibly abstract, Mitchell goes on to explain that:

“That the scale and extension of transportation lines and energy networks, along with urban development, irrigation projects, and other immense schemes, depended not just on material durability but upon the durable arrangements of law, authority, compulsion, and justification.”

Sudan, though often imagined as a colonial backwater, was the site of one of the British Empire’s largest investments in industrial agriculture ever. The giant Gezira irrigated agricultural scheme, one of the only monuments to colonialism visible from outer space, was originally planned in the 1920s to irrigate more than a million acres. British officials spoke openly of the Gezira Scheme’s potential to be a second man-made Nile Delta, a giant cotton farm for the Empire. From the 1920s until the scheme ran into financial problems in the 1970s, the railways, dams, ports and even Sudan’s labor force were geared to serve this project, not to mention the country’s financial and economic infrastructure.

This changed in the 1990s as the oil sector rose to prominence, but even then, pipelines and refineries tended to be located according to patterns established during the colonial era. These patterns endured in part because irrigation canals and railways cut into the earth and were reinforced with steel, and because Sudan integrated into global financial markets through loans for investments backed by access to export markets. Originally, it was cotton, later crude oil and now gold.

The Fragile Liberal International Order

When the Princeton political scientist G. John Ikenberry wrote about the liberal international order, he remarked that, “there is an optimist assumption lurking in liberal internationalism that states can overcome constraints and cooperate to solve security dilemmas, pursue collective action, and create an open, stable system.” Yet Ikenberry also admits that the system’s collective nature was always more aspirational than practical. Ikenberry admits that since 1945 the United States has served as the owner and operator of this system and has been afforded special privileges and responsibilities. Applebaum describes the chaos that unfolds in Sudan once the United States is no longer willing to bear its historic burden. Read Noema in print.

“Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era.”

But what if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable? While cotton and crude petroleum are different commodities, the central state could largely control their export, either by managing production directly or by issuing licenses for production and sale to favored clients. The boom in gold exports from Sudan since 2013 is remarkable because of the state’s utter inability to control the trade. For Sudan, the tragedy is magnified by the almost 200% rise in gold prices during that period, meaning the Sudanese state lost out on this windfall due to incapacity and now war. Part of the challenge for Sudanese authorities is that artisanal gold production , unlike control of oilfields and pipelines or cotton irrigation, lacks the central infrastructural chokepoints the colonial and postcolonial state had become so adept at taxing.

The other dilemma for the Sudanese state is the regional collapse of the taboo against dealing with subnational actors. As a result, gold from the mines of Darfur often ends up in the souks of Dubai without ever passing through the central government. Similarly, Sudanese soldiers guarding the Saudi-Yemeni border can be hired and deployed without ever contracting with the SAF. The RSF, a paramilitary-slash-merchant company, carries out many of these transactions, managing large portions of Sudan on behalf of its investors.

Precolonial Patterns Return In Contemporary Guises

What looks like chaos reveals patterns. In the 3 ½ years since fighting broke out between the SAF and the RSF, new trade and military supply routes have become increasingly visible. During the first few decades following Sudan’s independence in 1956, most economic activity flowed from the provinces to Khartoum, then along the railroad lines to Port Sudan on the Red Sea. The government earned most of its revenue by taxing the imports and exports that followed this well-trodden route. During the first two years of fighting, the Rapid Support Forces controlled Khartoum and did everything in their power to break the old colonial trade route. During this time, Sudan’s government retreated to Port Sudan, and the RSF set up a rival capital in Nyala in southern Darfur.

Inadvertently, the war revealed older patterns of state formation from the 19th century. Sudan’s city of Suakin and its other Red Sea ports claimed allegiance to a distant Ottoman government and resisted incorporation into the Kingdom of Sennar, to say nothing of Darfur. Elites in Suakin often sought incorporation into the Ottoman province of the Hijaz or Aden on the Arabian Peninsula. This pattern threatened to repeat itself when Sudan’s government was again temporarily forced to relocate to Port Sudan after Khartoum fell in 2023.

But perhaps more dramatically, the war saw the re-emergence of old trade routes to the north, west and south of Darfur. With the SAF in control of Port Sudan, the RSF began to turn to the old trade routes across the desert, the most famous of which was the Darb El Arba’īn, or “40 Day Road,” leading from northern Darfur to Asyut in southern Egypt. Other trade routes led north into Libya, where the RSF is suspected to have established bases under the protection of the Libyan militia leader who rules the eastern part of the country, Khalifa Haftar. Similarly, the trading routes from southern Darfur into South Sudan have been reactivated to resupply the RSF. These routes often end in Uganda, Kenya and the Central African Republic. All outside the control of the center.

The new prominence of the old trade routes was capped by the declaration of TASIS , or the Sudan Founding Alliance, of a new government in April 2025, exactly two years after the outbreak of the war. Speaking from Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, TASIS leaders tried to solidify an alliance between the RSF, parts of the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), a militant group and political party, and the leadership of the Baggara confederation. The Baggara includes more than six million Arab and African people stretching from southern Kordofan to Lake Chad.

The RSF’s organization, founded in 2013 — with the Darfurian Arab family of its leader Muhammad Hamdan Daglo Musa at its center — itself echoes an episode from the late 19th century. The first is the creation of a private-merchant empire by al-Zubayr Rahma al-Mansur, usually known as Zubayr Pasha . Originally a lackluster merchant assistant for an Egyptian trader, by the 1860s Zubayr had established one of the largest merchant companies operating in what we today refer to as South Sudan.

His operations were described in a remembrance in the “Middle East Monitor” as such: “[He sent] men ‘through the lands of the Dinka, Jur and Bongo, the company reached the Golo, then living between the Kuru and Kpongo rivers.’ They purchased ostrich feathers and ivory for trade in Khartoum, Cairo and beyond.” By the 1870s, he had grown from a successful trader into the ruler of a territory often called Deim Zubayr, controlling a large area of present-day South Sudan’s Bahr al-Ghazal and Darfur with an army of some 12,000 soldiers, many of whom were enslaved. According to the historian Tsega Etefa , writing in the Journal of Oromo Studies:

“What if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable?”

“By the late 1860s, al Zubayr was ‘the most prominent and successful of the merchant princes operating in the Bahr al-Ghazal.’ He traded in slaves and ivory; however, antislavery movements by Egyptian and European explorers in the Nile Valley began to put pressure on him. Therefore, ‘he arranged with the Baqqara tribes of southern Darfur for his slave caravans to pass through their territory northward, bypassing the Nile.’ Toward the end of the 1860s, ‘he attained the position of practically an independent ruler.’ The Egyptian government’s expeditionary force ‘was completely defeated by him, and the Egyptian authorities, realizing with what a commanding character they were confronted, made him Governor of the district.’”

Initially, Zubayr’s base was in the southern borderlands between Darfur and Bahr al-Ghazal. Darfur, as an independent political entity, was not conquered until 1874, when Zubayr’s forces achieved what the Ottoman-Egyptian armies of Muhammad Ali had been unable to do in 1821: conquering the Fur Sultanate at its capital of El Fasher. The parallels with the RSF appear to write themselves. These became particularly notable when the RSF took El Fasher after months of siege at the end of October 2025. In the process, the RSF captured the last major stronghold in Darfur and solidified their ability to resupply to the north through Libya and to the south across the expanse of South Sudan into East Africa.

Yet another echo of the 19th century was the emergence of Kordofan as a contested region. The armies of Muhammad Ali, de facto ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, partially pacified the region in the decades after the 1821 invasion from Egypt, but could not maintain stable control. In many ways, this resembles the situation in Kordofan today, where cities like El-Obeid , with a population over 600,000, remain under frequent attack as rival forces contend to dominate the region. Still, the 19th-century echoes perhaps become clearest in the relative autonomy of the SPLM-N, a political party and militant group with its strongholds based in southern Kordofan.

The SPLM-N has been both a broker and spoiler for South Sudan since its secession in 2011. The flat plains were easily conquered, but the Nuba Mountains were very difficult to ultimately control. One faction, SPLM-N Al-Hilu, which mostly controls the areas around the Nuba Mountains in South Kordofan, sided with the RSF, while another faction, SPLM-N Agar, which controls parts of the Blue Nile state, has sided with the SAF.

In the process, the two groups have maintained the autonomy of the border regions between the RSF, SAF and South Sudan. A borderland organization more interested in preserving its own autonomy than in the outcome of the war has found itself operating on both sides of the conflict. In this way, they are implementing strategies with other surprising parallels in the past, such as the Kingdom of Taqali , a kingdom in the northeastern Nuba Mountains of Sudan that flourished between about 1780 and 1884, with relative autonomy that extended well into Sudan’s post-independence period until 1969.

Our research in the Sudan Collection at the University of Bergen in Norway shows that during the 19th century, Taqali leaders used a similar strategy of seeking protection and recognition from both the waning states of Darfur and Sennar — pledging vassalage to both simultaneously as they worked to maintain autonomy.

The breakdown of the Sudanese state we are witnessing today is also not random. Rather, along with the retreat of the liberal world order, we are witnessing the reappearance of political orders that last manifested themselves with such clarity in the 19th century. These patterns repeat because they are based on trade and political and economic linkages that do not rely on the infrastructure built during the colonial period. The durability of this infrastructure has decayed as the institutions of the liberal world order that maintained it have crumbled. In the place of the patterns of trade, infrastructure and political order that once felt like inevitable parts of the postcolonial world, we are witnessing the reappearance of the older routes of exchange.

For instance, we see the re-emergence of the Trans-Saharan routes, the trading routes into East and Central Africa and East-West connections across the Sahel and the Red Sea. In South Africa, there are calls to dissolve the Union of South Africa, which in 1910 joined the British Cape Colony with the independent Boer republics of the Transvaal and Free State as well as Natal. Yemen has been redividing for over a decade now in ways that are reminiscent of the 19th century, and of course Russian aggression has called into question the stability of eastern Europe’s borders.

These are just a few examples of how the stability that defined the second half of the 20th century cannot be taken for granted. As we think of what models might best explain statecraft after the liberal order, it increasingly makes sense to look at the 19th-century map as an example of political competition and shifting boundaries.

stories.title: When The Present Eats The Future
stories.summary: The post When The Present Eats The Future appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Achilles heel of consumer democracies.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The Achilles heel of consumer democracies is that there is precious little constituency for the future in the present. All the feedback signals — in politics, culture and the market — are geared to short-term gratification. In each case, the incentives of the system deliver what the most influential demographic wants, and when they want it, which is now.

From fast fashion to electoral contests to quarterly earnings reports, the system is responsive to the pursuit of happiness defined by the near horizon.

The consequence of this, which Harvard sociologist Daniel Bell argued more than half a century ago in his book, “The Cultural Contradictions of Capitalism,” is that the present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society. The recent Noema essay by Simon Curtis and Ian Klaus titled “Americans Are Losing The Long Game” is excellent on this point.

While state-guided dirigiste policies that champion and support strategic industries deemed critical for the future are roundly frowned upon in market economies, the opposite rigidity of the short-term consumerist mentality is less appreciated as a critical failure of good governance. Yet, unless societies prepare for, subsidize and invest in the kind of future they want, they will never get there.

“The present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society.”

China’s Market-State Modality

Of all the major powers, post-Mao China stands out in taking control of its future without sacrificing the present. Over recent decades, it has both lifted hundreds of millions into general prosperity while, at the same time, swiftly conquering the key industries of a sustainable future, from green technology to artificial intelligence.

One has to admit that the Middle Kingdom’s mix of a long-term planning framework checked by robust market signals and bolstered by strategically deployed subsidies has worked. Indeed, it has worked too well: Its overproduction is spilling out and flooding world markets, threatening to displace domestic jobs and industry elsewhere.

China has not arrived at this point overnight. It has been a long time coming. In 1987, the ideology chief of the Communist Party politburo at the time, Hu Qili, told me in Beijing: “The market is not a feature unique to capitalism. Capitalism does not have the patent right over the market economy. What we are trying to create is a new and unprecedented modality where planning is combined with the commodity economy, where the state regulates the market, and the market guides the enterprises.”

The overall economy is steered by a one-party political system designed to reach consensus over long-term goals that have the decisive thrust to be carried out over many years without a break in continuity. Once set, the policy path is followed with relative discipline by a leadership and administration that, while not based on popular appeal to an electorate, is systemically accountable for realizing its set objectives.

When a key strategic goal is ordained by the Party, the state fosters a “whole dragon” approach in which start-up subsidies, sourcing, supply chains and production capacity are vertically aligned, making it one of the most powerful production ensembles in economic history.

Flaws Linked To Strength

The chief flaw of China’s system, of course, is closely linked to its strength. To keep the consensus from fraying, it overcompensates on the side of repressive order and control of freedom. It is the opposite of the open societies of the West, where the flaw lies within the strength of diverse participation and electoral competition: a growing inability to forge a consensus on long-term goals out of the cacophony of voices, the welter of contending interests and the immediate wash of fickle public opinion.

When all-out competitive partisanship destroys consensus among the body politic, the democratic transfer of power can mean a complete rupture of policies endorsed by most voters only four years earlier. Sticking to the course for the time it takes to reach fruition is not a reliable feature of this system.

The extreme edge of this stark difference can be seen in the contrasting behavior of the current leadership in the U.S. and China. America’s leader relishes dominating the memes of the moment, battling his way through every 24-hour news cycle by firing off social media barrages at sundry foes. China’s near-dictatorial leader has used his amassed clout to chart out a roadmap for the next half century.

China’s Long March To Owning Green Technologies

Meeting in Mexico in 2012, the G-20 decided for the first time to put climate change on the agenda. In those days, the Berggruen Institute’s 21 st Century Council, a group of former heads of state and government, tech leaders and Nobel laureates, would meet with the chair of the G-20 each year to advise on its agenda. Read Noema in print.

That year’s chair, then Mexican president Felipe Calderón, invited the council for lunch in the garden of Los Pinos, the presidential palace, to discuss the upcoming meeting. When the topic turned to climate, Wu Jianmin, a top Chinese diplomat and executive director of the China Institute for Innovation and Development Strategy, related that a top priority of the then incoming Party leadership of Xi Jinping would be “ecological civilization.”

All those 14 years ago, he confidently laid out a trajectory of China’s decisive shift to electric vehicles and plans for massive R&D investment in battery storage for wind and solar as well as EVs. Everyone listened respectfully, but doubtfully, because China was then not even in the auto race.

In 2012, China already dominated solar panels, but the Chevy Volt was the world’s most produced EV. No nation commanded battery production, which then was only nascently entering global competition.

Wu’s confidence in China’s capacity to deliver was well-founded. Today, nearly 70% of all new car sales in China are EVs, and half of all sales globally are Chinese-made electric vehicles. China produces around 80% of the world’s batteries and holds 70% of global battery patents. Its hosts half of the entire world’s large-scale battery storage capacity, primarily to store solar and wind power for the grid when the sun isn’t shining or the wind blowing.

As part of its whole-dragon approach, China also built out the widely distributed infrastructure of rapid charging stations across the country necessary to boost EV use. It launched a strategic push to link battery storage to the grid, requiring developers to build or commission large-scale storage capacity as a condition for approval of new wind or solar installations.

China’s export of its technology has enabled the advance of large-scale batteries for integration into power grids in many countries. Some 70% of EV batteries worldwide are from China.

California has the most installed large battery storage facilities outside of China. Its capacity has grown from a mere 700 megawatts in 2019 to 21,000 MW in 2026. By 2045, the state aims to reach 52,000 MW capacity to support a 100% clean energy grid. For the entire month of May 2026, 51% of California’s total energy demand came from solar power. Blackouts during the intense heatwaves of recent years have been avoided because the grid was linked to off-hour battery storage from renewable energy.

Though often assembled in California, 90% of the cells and core components of the large-scale batteries the state has installed come from China.

Quotas And Dumping

From the standpoint of the race against time on climate, the widest possible dispersion of China’s green technology is a net plus for the planet. Yet, as in other realms of trade competition, its cheaper product and overproduction portends a vulnerable dependence on a political system which the West considers a strategic adversary.

To the extent domestic industries exist, China’s prowess threatens to run them out of business. Since green technology is critical to our future, the most sensible approach would not be to prohibit Chinese imports, but set a reasonable quota beyond which tariffs would kick in. That would both limit the damage while allowing competition from abroad to spark the scale-up of domestic industry.

Free-market ideologues aside, subsidies are not the end of the world when a livable biosphere is at stake. After all, up until the Trump administration, the U.S. did manage for a time to escape the pull of consumer immediacy. For years, it subsidized the purchase of EVs with tax rebates. And California has shown how regulation creates, not destroys, markets. Elon Musk’s Tesla empire would never have emerged if it were not for the state’s fuel efficiency and clean energy standards, which created the market for his technology.

“Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China?”

Is It Impolitic To Learn From China?

Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China? This is not, of course, to imply in any way that the West turn toward autocracy or authoritarianism. It is only to warn that unless democracies can look beyond the short-term horizon and find ways to reach a governing consensus that sticks, they will be left in the dust of the oncoming future.

To turn an old Chinese saying toward ourselves: “The stones from hills yonder can polish jade at home.”

stories.body:
Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons

For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.

Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.

The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.

It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border , named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.

“China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.

Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin ’s war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked.

In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally China .

North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.

However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’s nuclear weapons programme .

In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”

The North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. In 2024, the North said it would sever all rail and road links with its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country’s “ principal enemy ”.

But Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, citing Kim’s refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in Moscow and Beijing.

“Both countries understand that Kim Jong-un would rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”

Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.

“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”

The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.

Tertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges will bring means improvements to the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”

Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first. But it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.

“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Building pylons in Wales could be a thing of the past, with the country's ministers instead wanting to bury energy cables underground

Published 23 October 2026

The Welsh government has announced plans to ban the use of traditional steel pylons to support electricity lines over which it has control.

Plaid Cymru ministers favour burying cables underground instead.

Plans for a network of pylons in the Towy Valley have faced a fierce local backlash with local Plaid politicians speaking out against the proposals.

The company behind the plans, Green Gen Cymru, said it welcomed the consultation and that it supported using "the right infrastructure in the right place".

Prohibiting the use of large steel lattice pylons for new lines up to 132 kilovolts was a Plaid Cymru manifesto pledge before May's Senedd election.

Launching a consultation on its policy on Friday, the Welsh government said undergrounding electricity circuits could "reduce the visual impact of electricity infrastructure, helping to protect landscapes and local amenity".

It also said that burying cables could make them less vulnerable to severe weather and could reduce the potential impact on birds and other wildlife.

However, the consultation document also acknowledges that undergrounding was "generally considered more expensive to install and maintain and could create construction impacts during installation".

The government's policy would allow for wooden poles or "equivalent, less intrusive infrastructure" to be used to support overhead cables where undergrounding isn't feasible.

Farmers 'vindicated' after judge's ruling on pylon firm accessing land Published 6 July

Energy firm unveils new slimline pylons designed 'with Welsh landscape in mind' after backlash Published 17 September

Green Gen has plans to build three major power line routes connecting onshore wind farms planned by its sister company Bute Energy with the wider grid network.

It has previously said it would invest nearly £1bn by 2030, with proposals affecting parts of Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Powys and Shropshire.

But it has faced considerable opposition in certain communities, with groups representing hundreds of landowners taking the company to court in 2025 .

In a bid to address concerns, Green Gen recently unveiled a "slim and compact" 22 metre (72ft) pylon, designed "with the Welsh landscape in mind".

The company has consistently said that undergrounding its cables would cost on average 4.5 times more , external than running them overhead.

That would mean an extra cost of £500m for the Towy Usk project between Carmarthenshire and Powys, according to Green Gen.

Green Gen Cymru has proposed three pylon routes from mid Wales across to Shropshire, south-west Wales to Ceredigion, and one from the same point to Powys

Welsh Energy Minister Adam Price said: "We know the necessary changes in the way energy is generated and used in Wales will require new grid infrastructure, however, we also know that new infrastructure can impact on the communities and the environment that hosts it.

"We want to see infrastructure that is sensitively designed to minimise impacts on the environment and the communities that host them, while offering the maximum benefits for Wales."

Andrew Hardcastle, executive director at Green Gen Cymru, said: "We welcome the Welsh government's consultation and its recognition of the importance of delivering the electricity infrastructure Wales needs in a way that is sensitive to our landscapes, environment and communities.

"Like all grid companies across the UK, we believe there is no one-size-fits-all solution to developing new electricity networks.

"Our approach is to use the right infrastructure in the right place, drawing on a range of technologies including underground cables, wooden poles and our recently announced lower-profile monopoles."

The company said it was "pleased that the consultation recognises the potential role of less visually intrusive overhead infrastructure, including monopoles, and invites evidence on their use".

Reform's Senedd spokesperson for rural affairs, Laura Anne Jones, said: "As part of our energy policy, we will continue to push for new power lines to be placed underground wherever possible, protecting our landscapes and rural communities.

"Reform will always stand up for our countryside and fight against its industrialisation."

Welsh Labour's environment, rural affairs, energy and transport spokesperson, Vikki Howells said: "Burying cables can cost five times as much as overhead lines, making electric more expensive and decarbonisation more difficult."

She said the sensible position was choosing the right engineering solution for the right landscape and "undergrounding should absolutely remain available where landscape, environmental or other circumstances justify it".

The Welsh Conservatives welcomed the policy consultation.

The party's environment spokesperson, Andrew RT Davies said: "We recognise that Wales needs a modern electricity network to support economic growth, but communities should not have to accept eyesores across our beautiful natural landscapes, which must be conserved."

The consultation , external will run until 15 January 2027.

Dyfan Walters called it a "positive day" for campaigners

Eirian Edwards, a campaigner in the Llandovery Pylon Group, said: "We welcome that they are seriously looking at undergrounding as the preferred option - to protect landscapes and people's livelihoods.

"If infrastructure has to be planned, then we're not against that process at all. We realise that we need to strengthen our local grid, but certain projects that are planned do not fulfil that at all."

Dyfan Walters, a farmer in Llandovery who is also a member of Llandovery Pylon Group, called it "a positive day for us".

"We're fully supportive and understand that the infrastructure is required.

"Putting that underground means that there's less impact on agriculture, less impact on tourism.

"In a world where there's an ever-changing climate, having that resilience - having infrastructure placed underground - is a sensible way forward."

stories.body:
Jack Ross (pictured) held the post of Chief Operations Officer at Turning Point UK, an offshoot of the US organisation

Published 24 October 2026, 03:52 BST

A former Tory activist who appeared to offer to "broker" the hiring of contract killers in an undercover film report previously worked for Conservative headquarters.

Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.

It comes after Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch referred to them as "shocking allegations", adding that she did not "believe that person is a member anymore".

A Conservative spokesman said Ross's party membership had "been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation". It has reported that Ross said his words were not meant to be taken seriously.

Ross was paid to provide social media advice to the party for a brief period, the BBC has been told. He was never an employee or Conservative Campaign Headquarters pass holder.

However, he met Badenoch on several occasions as part of his role as chief executive of Turning Point UK, an offshoot of a right-wing American organisation.

Ross has also met several other right-wing politicians including the former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.

In undercover filming broadcast this week by Al Jazeera, Ross appears to offer to "broker" the services of contract killers.

The Al Jazeera report said its undercover journalist approached Ross in 2022 with a fictitious situation of a family business at risk of being taken over by a criminal gang.

Ross is alleged to have asked the undercover reporter what was needed from him, and listed violent options that could be bought including stabbing, shooting and killing.

Al Jazeera said Ross denied the finding "completely" and claimed everything he said to the reporter was not meant seriously.

Turning Point UK has been approached for comment.

Storm Adam brings torrential rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen strikes England and Wales

Storm Adam brought torrential rain to eastern Spain earlier this week. In Pego, Alicante, 632mm fell in 36 hours, with 430mm of this falling in just six hours, while the Valencian town of Olivia received 600mm in 24 hours.

The severe flooding led 145 municipalities across Valencia and Alicante to impose a temporary lockdown on about 850,000 people on Monday. At least five people have died, 500 have been rescued and 2,100 evacuated.

The storm also affected the Balearic Islands, with more than 130 incidents recorded in Ibiza including standing water at the airport causing some flights to be diverted or suspended. Although the worst of the storm has passed and conditions are improving across Valencia and Alicante, local disruption is expected to continue.

The first named storm of the winter for the UK is tracking through the Channel. Storm Austen is bringing damaging winds not only to south-west England and Wales, but south-west Ireland and northern France. Gusts are expected to be around 50-60mph, but some exposed north-western coasts of France could experience winds of up to 80-90mph.

Following quickly on from Storm Austen is another deep low-pressure system, Storm Boelo, which is expected to track across northern Scotland on Saturday into Sunday. Much of the UK and Ireland will experience very unsettled conditions with further damaging winds, and heavy and prolonged rain. Western Scotland will face the strongest gusts, but the rest of the UK and Ireland can expect 40-55mph winds. Western parts of Ireland will experience 50-60mph winds with up to 70-80mph in exposed parts of north-west Ireland, similar to western Scotland. Again, heavy rain associated with Storm Boelo will reach 10-20mm, with as much as 30-60mm in western parts of Ireland, Wales and south-west England. This, on top of the rainfall from Storm Austen, will increase the risk of flooding.

Super Typhoon Champi is heading towards China and Japan over the weekend after passing north-eastern Taiwan on Friday. It has weakened since Wednesday, but is still a significant typhoon with the equivalent strength of a category 5 hurricane, producing 185mph gusts and sustained winds of 121 mph. After torrential rain from the typhoon this week, up to 900mm of rain is forecast to fall in the mountainous regions of northern and eastern Taiwan from Tuesday to Saturday. As a result, there are school closures, cancelled flights and six-metre waves, with damage expected over the next few days.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, with at least seven aftershocks recorded

A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit Tibet , killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and destroying hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media have said.

Search and rescue efforts continued after at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds collapsed, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, according to China’s national broadcaster CCTV.

More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed to help rescue efforts. Supplies were also sent into the region, including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,000 tents, folding beds, torches and winter clothing.

The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 119 miles (191km) east-north-east of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 11 miles.

The agency recorded at least seven aftershocks of magnitudes between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 6 miles. Videos posted by CCTV showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.

China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to stop trains passing through the region.

More than 300 police officers were dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue services had sent almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported. Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.

The earthquake caused rockfalls, forcing local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua. Intermittent snow was expected in the region over the next three days, Xinhua said.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, called for an all-out effort in the rescue operation and medical relief work.

Nagqu is more than 185 miles north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa. Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.

In August, a disastrous flood hit the border of Tibet and Nepal. China’s tight grip on information prevented international media from visiting the affected regions on the Tibetan side, obscuring the scale of the damage.

In December 2023, a quake in remote Gansu province in north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.

Tibet is a particularly seismically active area. The high-altitude region was taken under Chinese control in the 1950s and its people, who are predominantly ethnic Tibetans, have had a tense relationship with the authorities in Beijing since. As well as being one of the poorest regions in China, many Tibetans reject Beijing-imposed controls on their culture and religion.

stories.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
stories.summary: The chancellor will unveil AI spending aimed at shoring up the UK's defences in Wednesday's Budget.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 October 2026, 01:05 BST

The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.

As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.

The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.

"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."

The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.

"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.

"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."

The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it? Published 14 September

Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says Published 1 day ago

The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).

Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.

The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.

It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.

This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.

It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.

There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.

But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

stories.title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
stories.summary: Do British pensioners have it better or worse than those in other countries?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 October 2026, 01:09 BST

Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.

The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.

But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.

Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.

And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.

Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.

But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries?

One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate.

The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.

On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries.

And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes.

If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.

Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care Published 29 September

State pension likely to top £13,000 a year Published 15 September

What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it? Published 29 September

But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows.

However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.

So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK?

Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund.

But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.

But there are two issues to consider.

Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.

And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes).

Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing.

As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.

So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap.

The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.

It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men.

But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.

Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.

So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere.

But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action.

The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.

That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

stories.title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
stories.summary: The US president has praised Burnham after the government allowed gas drilling in the North Sea's Jackdaw field.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Donald Trump said Andy Burnham's decision on Jackdaw would "make the UK a very rich country"

Published 23 October 2026

US President Donald Trump has praised Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the UK government's decision to approve production from the North Sea's Jackdaw gas field.

He said he had spoken with Burnham, telling reporters on Friday that the decision would "make the UK a very rich country".

Trump said: "The other prime minister, the previous man, Starmer. He's a very nice man, but he never got it done, and this one is getting it."

The decision had been subject to intense debate around its environment and economic impact and came after years of legal challenges.

The Jackdaw platform is located east of Aberdeen

Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.

Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.

He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."

Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."

In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.

The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.

It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".

Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed.

However, Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision by not giving any regard to climate obligations - things he said "have to be considered in the round".

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month, but that it would not lower energy bills this winter.

She said the decision was "compatible" with legally binding climate commitments, adding: "We remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050."

Environmental groups have criticised the Jackdaw approval. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said it was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Meanwhile, Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments".

During their Friday talks, Trump and Burnham spoke about the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between British and Israeli companies.

In September, the Argentinian government threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands, and earlier this month, it began legal action to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields.

Burnham raised the "economic consequences of Argentina's coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the Islanders' right to develop their natural resources", Downing Street said.

The two leaders also discussed Ukraine, with the prime minister underlining the importance for Ukraine "to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", according to Number 10.

Starlink technology is a satellite system owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company which Ukraine has relied upon during the war.

In recent days, Ukraine has been recording issues with the network , according to sources within the defence ministry. This has affected the country's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.

The Downing Street statement added: "The Prime Minister recognised the work of President Trump to bring Putin to the negotiation table and the leaders agreed to work together, alongside international partners to bring an end to the bloodshed."

stories.title: Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
stories.summary: Green leaders have been given until Sunday to disown their party's "Zionism is racism" conference vote.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Green leader Zack Polanski has faced criticism over his response to the Zionism motion

Published 23 October 2026

Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism.

The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power.

Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end.

But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse.

The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made.

These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition.

The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council.

In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum.

In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it.

But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party.

In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio.

Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded.

The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first.

Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford.

Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum.

Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023.

The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy.

Conference motion

The "Zionism is racism" motion was passed by members of the Green Party of England and Wales at its annual conference in Brighton last month.

The policy motion adopted by members said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.

It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs.

Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.

Labour councillors require the approval of the party's NEC before entering into local tie-ups.

According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power-sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office.

By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally.

A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong.

"Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic."

stories.title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets
stories.summary: Anthony Lee passed confidential information to his wife Laura Lee about when the 2024 general election would be held.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Anthony Lee and his wife Laura pleaded guilty at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday

Published 23 October 2026

The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have received suspended prison sentences after they admitted to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.

Anthony Lee used "inside information" emerging from a private meeting called by then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to bet on the general election date months before it took place, Southwark Crown Court heard.

Lee and his wife Laura stood to win more than £23,000 had their cheating not been uncovered, the court heard.

Lee was sentenced to 10 months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, while his wife was sentenced to four months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for a year.

Amy Hind, a former Tory party employee who was working as an NHS business support manager, was also sentenced to six months' imprisonment, suspended for a year, after previously pleading guilty to cheating on the date of the election.

Judge Tony Baumgartner, sentencing the three of them, said their conduct "risked undermining" the confidence the public has in the Conservative Party "as an institution", "undermining trust in the democratic process" and the "integrity of the gambling system".

The trio were among several people charged with betting offences by the Gambling Commission.

The trials of other defendants will take place next year and in 2028.

Former Conservative MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.

'Profit for themselves'

Sunak's decision to call a general election for July 2024 was a surprise to many, including several Conservative MPs, who were expecting an autumn date.

The court heard that Sunak held a private Downing Street meeting on 10 March of that year to discuss possible dates.

Neither Lee nor his wife attended the meeting, but the couple began betting online on the election being held in July or between July and September, the court heard.

Prosecutor Zoe Johnson said: "Although not at Number 10, the overwhelming inference is that Anthony Lee was receiving inside information as the meeting went on and was acting upon it."

She added: "Together they were using it to make a profit for themselves."

Lee placed or tried to place 71 bets during the period, while his wife placed eight and attempted a ninth, the court heard.

Baumgartner described Anthony Lee as a "central figure" in the preparation of the general election, who sat at a group of desks within Tory HQ known as the "God Pod".

Representing Lee, barrister Richard Pratt said his client did not concretely know the working date of the election, saying it "still represented a gamble from his point of view".

The barrister told the court: "It was always possible the prime minister could change his mind."

Pratt said there "wasn't any direct manipulation" by the defendant.

Laura Lee worked for the Tories as their "head of international" and had been selected as the party candidate for Bristol North West for the election.

Baumgartner said she had no involvement in the election planning and her access to information "came predominantly" from her husband.

The court heard Hind's husband Anthony worked as a deputy digital director for the Conservatives but did not place any bets himself.

Baumgartner said Hind's husband "was party to emails relating to the forthcoming general election and was one potential source of your inside information".

The judge later said "someone else who worked within the heart of CCHQ" could have given her the "highly confidential" information.

The court heard Hind placed four bets and made three further unsuccessful attempts to place bets. The unsuccessful attempts were for £767, £700 and £750.

The judge described Hind's bets as a "clear departure from your previous betting history", noting: "Before the present offending, your largest stake had been £10.50, and only seven of your 3,399 recorded selections involved a stake of that amount."

'Justice has been served'

Neither of the defendants have previous convictions and they are all of good previous character, the court heard.

Baumgartner described them all as having expressed remorse for their actions.

The trio are now subject to a 12-month prohibited activity requirement, banning them from accessing or using online gambling websites or applications.

Anthony Lee was ordered to complete 100 hours of unpaid work and pay more than £6,600 in compensation to a betting company, while Laura Lee must carry out 40 hours of unpaid work and pay £4,265.

Hind was ordered to complete 50 hours of unpaid work.

Katharine Diamond, General Counsel of regulators the Gambling Commission, reacted to the sentencing of the trio by saying "justice has been served".

She described the case as "a first of its kind" and said it demonstrated the commission's "commitment to protecting the integrity of betting markets".

stories.title: Police yet to receive £2m after A66 crash, says commissioner
stories.summary: Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey says it has been nearly two months since force was promised the cash.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Seven people including two police officers were killed in the crash on the A66 in the early hours of 22 August

Published 22 October 2026

A police force has still not received the £2m it was promised by the government in the wake of a car crash that led to the deaths of seven people, including two police officers, the local police and crime commissioner (PCC) says.

Cleveland PCC Matt Storey said Cleveland Police was still waiting for the extra funding promised by the home secretary in August.

Shabana Mahmood pledged the cash in light of challenges faced by the force following the deaths, which followed a pursuit on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.

The Home Office said the force would receive the £2m it had been promised by the end of November.

During the fatal crash, a Volkswagen Passat in which the five young men were travelling hit an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the dual carriageway near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST.

Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died at the scene.

The occupants of the VW Passat, which was travelling the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy - were also killed.

On the morning of the crash, Cleveland Police said it received several reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 had been seen ramming properties.

Further arrests were subsequently made in connection with organised crime, including the following weekend after another vehicle ramming.

PCC Matt Storey called for the £2m to be released immediately

Storey called for the immediate release of the £2m but also said policing costs linked to the crash, which had led to the arrests of 50 people so far, were now forecast to exceed £5m.

"These are exceptional and unavoidable costs arising from utterly tragic and devastating circumstances," he said.

"They are not costs that should be borne locally or met from existing policing budgets."

The PCC also criticised the lack of a "substantive" communication from the government about Cleveland Police's long-term funding.

Storey said the current police funding model, which Mahmood had previously committed to reviewing, disadvantaged the Teesside force.

He said the upcoming Budget was a chance to "align resources more fairly with demand" and "place Cleveland on a sustainable footing".

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in the crash in August

The 50 arrests have come as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash.

Fifteen people have been charged - 13 men and two women ranging in age from 19-45.
